title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can write the code that reads a file into R. It knows every function and every argument. What it cannot do is:

see the files on your computer
know what is inside them
know what the data is for
tell whether the result is right

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: what importing and exporting are, and what has to be true for them to work
Reading code: recognising what a line of import code does, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in your request
Checking: how to tell whether the code the AI wrote did the right thing




Clone this repository, which holds the datasets used here
Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse, haven and here packages if you have not already. Installing is a one-time step per computer (see the packages slide in Chapter 1).

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
text:
How reading code is written
A data file is a table saved on disk in some format. Reading it means a function opens the file and builds a table inside R (R calls it a data frame; this deck says table) that you give a name to. Whatever the format, and whichever function the AI picks, the code follows the same pattern.

The patternEvery reader follows the patternOptionsVariations you will see



table_name <- reader_function("path/to/file", option = value, ...)









Part
What it is
Required?




table_name <-
The name the table will have inside R. <- stores the result under that name.
Needed to keep the result


reader_function
The function that understands the file’s format
Yes


"path/to/file"
Where the file is, always the first input
Yes, the only required input


option = value
Extra instructions about the layout and types
No; each has a default



A real line that follows the pattern:

corn <- read_csv("corn_yields.csv")

On these slides the data files sit in the same folder as the slides, so a path is just the file name. In your own project, paths are built with here::here() (see Condition 1).


Readers differ in name and package, not in pattern. The shortest call to each is the path and nothing else:








Format
Shortest call
Package




csv
read_csv("corn.csv")
readr (tidyverse)


csv
read.csv("corn.csv")
built into R


Excel
read_excel("corn.xlsx"), or read_xls(), read_xlsx()
readxl


STATA
read_dta("corn.dta")
haven


R’s own
readRDS("corn.rds")
built into R



The help pages call the first input file for some readers and path for others. The name differs; its position, first, does not.


Everything after the path is optional and written as name = value. Each option you leave out takes its default, a value chosen by whoever wrote the function. Options you will see, grouped by what they tell the reader:

Which part of the file: sheet = "corn_yields_08" (Excel), skip = 2 (ignore lines above the column names)
What marks a missing value: na = c("", ".", "-999") (for read.csv(), na.strings =)
What type each column is: col_types = ..., for example to keep an ID column as text




Important


A default is a guess about your file. When the guess is wrong, R gives no error, and that is where the silent failures later in this deck come from. Knowing what your file looks like is how you know which options the AI must set.





AI-written code often wraps the same pattern in extra pieces. They change how the line looks, not what it does:

readr::read_csv(...): the package name, then ::, then the function. Uses the function without loading the whole package.
read_csv(here::here("data", "corn.csv")): the path is built by another function instead of typed out (see Condition 1).
path <- here::here("data", "corn.csv") on one line, then read_csv(path) on the next: the path is stored first and used later.
read_csv(...) |> some_other_step(): the table is passed straight on to a next step (|>) before it is stored.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What has to be true for an import to work
text:
What has to be true for an import to work

The four conditionsFailures with and without an error



R can find the file. The path points at a file that exists.
The reader matches the format. A csv reader for a csv file, an Excel reader for an Excel file.
The reader understands the layout. Where the column names are, which sheet to read, what marks a missing value.
Each column gets the right type. Numbers as numbers, text as text, IDs kept exactly as written.




If condition 1 or 2 fails, R stops with an error. Annoying, but you know something is wrong.
If condition 3 or 4 fails, R gives you a table with no error, and the table is wrong. This deck calls these silent failures.




Important


The silent failures are why checking matters. Code that runs is not the same as code that is right.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 1: R can find the file
text:
Condition 1: R can find the file

PathsThe project root and here()Why AI gets this wrong


A path is the address of a file. There are two kinds:

Absolute path: starts at the top of the disk, for example "/Users/taro/Documents/class/corn_yields.csv". It works only on the computer it was written on, because nobody else has those folders.
Relative path: starts from the folder R is currently in (the working directory), for example "data/corn_yields.csv". It works only if R is in the folder you expected, and that folder changes:
At the Console: your project folder (if you opened an R Project, explained in the next tab)
Inside a .qmd file: the folder the .qmd is saved in

So "data/corn_yields.csv" can work at the Console and fail when a .qmd in analysis/ is rendered.


An R Project is a folder that RStudio marks with a .Rproj file; you open the project by opening that file. The top of that folder is the project root.
The safest path is one measured from the project root, whatever folder R is in. The here package does that: it finds the project root by looking for the .Rproj file. Recognise it when you see it:

corn <- read_csv(here::here("data", "corn_yields.csv"))

This reads data/corn_yields.csv inside your project, whichever subfolder your code is in and whoever’s computer it runs on. To check it is set up, run here::here() on its own at the Console: it should print your project folder.


The AI cannot see your folders, so it guesses the path. Its guesses tend to be one of these:

just the file name, assuming the file is in the working directory
an absolute path copied from an example, such as "C:/Users/yourname/..."
setwd(...) to change the working directory first

All three break as soon as the code runs somewhere else. Tell it where the file is (see “Asking AI” below).
If R says the file does not exist, send the AI the exact error message, the folder your .qmd is in, and where the file is inside your project.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Condition 2: the reader matches the format
text:
Condition 2: the reader matches the format
The file extension (the part after the last dot) tells you the format. Tell the AI the extension and it will pick a reader from the list under “How reading code is written”. What you need to know is what each format keeps, because that decides what can go wrong:








Extension
Format
What the file keeps




.csv
plain text, any software opens it
Only text. Types are guessed on reading.


.xls, .xlsx
Excel workbook
Several sheets per file; a reader takes the first unless told otherwise


.dta
STATA
Types, and a description stored with each column


.rds
R’s own format
The exact R object, nothing guessed






Note


A csv file stores everything as text, so the reader has to guess each column’s type. That guessing is where conditions 3 and 4 go wrong.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
text:
Conditions 3 and 4: the silent failures

Lost leading zerosCodes for missing valuesThe wrong sheet


County codes (FIPS) for Alabama start with 0. Here is a tiny csv, written straight into the code, and what the reader makes of it:

small_csv <- "fips,county,yield
01001,Autauga,150
01003,Baldwin,-999
31019,Buffalo,173"

small <- read_csv(I(small_csv), show_col_types = FALSE)
small$fips

[1] "01001" "01003" "31019"

read.csv(text = small_csv)$fips

[1]  1001  1003 31019


The two readers guessed differently about the same file. read_csv() kept 01001 as text. read.csv(), the built-in reader that AI assistants often write, decided the column was a number and turned 01001 into 1001. No error either way. Later, joining that table to another one by fips would quietly fail to match these counties.


The same file uses -999 to mean “no data”, a common convention. The reader does not know that:

mean(small$yield)

[1] -225.3333


An average yield of -225.3 bushels per acre, which is impossible. Again no error. The reader has to be told that -999 means missing.


corn_yields.xls has two sheets:

readxl::excel_sheets("corn_yields.xls")

[1] "corn_yields_08" "corn_yields_09"


A reader told nothing about sheets reads the first one only. If you wanted both years, you now have half the data, with no error.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
This is the way of working with AI that you should take into your own research. Every exercise in this course uses it, so that it is a habit by the time your thesis needs it.

You ask. Your request says what you want, what you know about the data, and which checks to print.
The AI writes into a Quarto document (.qmd). Code goes into code chunks, with one plain-English sentence above each chunk saying what it does and why.
You render the .qmd to HTML.
You read the HTML and decide whether the work is right: the sentences, the code, and the check results side by side.

Why this matters for research, and why you judge the HTML rather than the chat window:

Rendering runs every chunk from the top in a fresh R session. If the HTML is right, the analysis is reproducible; nothing depends on something typed into the Console and forgotten.
The HTML is a record of what was done to the data and why, with each explanation next to its code and its result. You can reread it months later, and your advisor or a coauthor can review your analysis by reading it, without running anything.
The chat disappears; the .qmd and its HTML stay with your project.




Note


Every request that asks for code ends with the same few lines telling the AI to work this way. This deck calls them the closing instructions; the full text is under Recommended requests near the end.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Look at the file before you ask
text:
Look at the file before you ask

WhyRaw first lines of a csvCounting lines


You cannot describe a file you have not looked at, and you cannot check an import without knowing what the file holds. Two ways to look:

Open it: a csv in a text editor, an Excel file in Excel
Ask R to show the raw first lines, before any reader has guessed anything




readLines("corn_yields.csv", n = 3)

[1] "Year,State,FIPS,County_name,State_name,Commodity,Data item,Irrigated,Yield"                         
[2] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",0,173"           
[3] "2008,31,31019,BUFFALO,NEBRASKA,CORN,\"CORN, GRAIN, IRRIGATED - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE\",1,182"


From this you learn: the first line is column names, values are separated by commas, FIPS is a 5-digit code, one column name (Data item) has a space in it.



length(readLines("corn_yields.csv"))

[1] 162


162 lines, one of which is the column names. So a correct import has 161 rows. Write that number down before you import.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: What to put in your request
text:
What to put in your request
The AI already knows the functions. Your request supplies what it cannot know, most of it from looking at the file:

The file: its name, its format, and where it sits inside your project
What is inside: the first few lines, the sheet names, and anything unusual (IDs with leading zeros, codes for missing values)
What you want back: the name of the table, what one row is, and which type each key column should be
Your project’s rules, if you have any beyond the closing instructions: for example, use the tidyverse
Ask for checks: have it print the numbers you will check against (next section)
The closing instructions: which .qmd and heading the code goes under, a sentence above each chunk, paths built with here::here(), checks printed as expected and got, and render to HTML





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the file and look for itself. Still write down what you expect (number of rows, types of key columns) before it runs, so you have something to compare against.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Read my corn data into R.
The AI has to guess the file name, its location, its format, its layout and what you want. A typical reply:

setwd("C:/Users/yourname/Documents")
corn <- read.csv("corn.csv")

It runs on nobody’s computer as written, and if you fix the path, it still guesses every type.


An example for a workbook with one sheet per year:
In my R project, the file data/corn_yields.xls is an Excel workbook with
two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09 (one per year). Each row is
one county, one year, and one irrigation status. I want both sheets
stacked into one table called corn, using the tidyverse, with FIPS kept
as text so leading zeros survive.

Then check the number of rows from each sheet (I expect 161 each), the
number of rows in corn (322), the type of every column, and the number
of missing values in each column (I expect none).

Put the code in my Quarto document analysis/import.qmd, under the
heading "Read the corn data", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write
one plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


What the AI’s answer looks like in the rendered HTML: a sentence, then the chunk it describes. Read each sentence and check that the code under it does what the sentence says.
Read both sheets, keeping every column as text so that FIPS keeps its leading zeros.

library(readxl)
library(dplyr)

path <- here::here("data", "corn_yields.xls")
corn_08 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_08", col_types = "text")
corn_09 <- read_excel(path, sheet = "corn_yields_09", col_types = "text")

Stack the two sheets into one table, then turn Year and Yield back into numbers, since they were read as text.

corn <- bind_rows(corn_08, corn_09) |>
  mutate(Year = as.integer(Year), Yield = as.numeric(Yield))

Print the checks: rows per sheet and in total, the type of every column, and missing values per column.

cat("rows in 2008 sheet: expected 161, got", nrow(corn_08), "\n")
cat("rows in 2009 sheet: expected 161, got", nrow(corn_09), "\n")
cat("rows in corn: expected 322, got", nrow(corn), "\n")
sapply(corn, class)
cat("missing values: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(corn)), "\n")

Two things to notice. library() loads a package so its functions can be used, and bind_rows() stacks one table on top of another (you will meet it properly later in this chapter). And the type check would show that State and Irrigated are still text, because only Year and Yield were turned back into numbers. That is the type check doing its job: you would ask the AI to make those two numbers as well.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking: what to ask for, and why
text:
Checking: what to ask for, and why

The five checksAsking for themReading the HTML


The AI can write the checking code. It cannot decide which checks your file needs, and it cannot know the right answers. Ask for these after every import:










Ask the AI to print
Why
What only you can supply




1
the number of rows and columns
Rows go missing or appear when the wrong sheet is read or a title line is read as data
the row count from looking at the file


2
the type of every column
A wrong guess (an ID read as a number, a number read as text) gives no error
which type each key column should be


3
the number of missing values in each column
A missing-value code the reader was not told about, such as -999, is kept as a real value
how the file marks missing values


4
the smallest and largest value of each numeric column
Impossible values expose those codes, and unit mistakes
what range is believable


5
the first row
Shifted or merged columns show up at once
the same row in the raw file





One sentence at the end of your request does it:
After reading the file, print: the number of rows and columns, the type of
every column, the number of missing values in each column, the smallest and
largest value of each numeric column, and the first row.
Better still, tell it what you expect, so the HTML says which checks passed:
I expect <number> rows, <number> columns, <ID columns> as text, <how many>
missing values, and <column> between <lowest> and <highest>. Print each
check on its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y".
The second version only works if you looked at the file first. That part only you can do.


For corn_yields.csv, the student expected 161 rows (from counting lines), 9 columns, FIPS as text, no missing values, and yields between 100 and 250. The AI wrote the code; in the rendered HTML, you read each line:


Code the AI wrote
cat(
  paste("rows: expected 161, got", nrow(corn)),
  paste("columns: expected 9, got", ncol(corn)),
  paste("type of FIPS: expected character, got", class(corn$FIPS)),
  paste("missing values: expected 0, got", sum(is.na(corn))),
  paste("Yield range: expected 100 to 250, got", min(corn$Yield), "to", max(corn$Yield)),
  paste("first row:", paste(unlist(corn[1, ]), collapse = ", ")),
  sep = "\n"
)


rows: expected 161, got 161
columns: expected 9, got 9
type of FIPS: expected character, got numeric
missing values: expected 0, got 0
Yield range: expected 100 to 250, got 103 to 204
first row: 2008, 31, 31019, BUFFALO, NEBRASKA, CORN, CORN, GRAIN - YIELD, MEASURED IN BU / ACRE, 0, 173



Rows, columns, missing values and the yield range match.
The first row matches the second line of the file (shown under “Look at the file before you ask”).
FIPS came back as a number, not the text you expected. In this file every code starts with 31, so nothing was lost, but the check fails, and you would ask the AI to read FIPS as text.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checks that come from knowing the data
text:
Checks that come from knowing the data
The five checks apply to any file. The most useful checks come from what you know about this data, and no AI will think of them for you.
In corn_yields.csv, most counties have two rows: one for irrigated corn and one for non-irrigated corn. Irrigated corn gets water that rain-fed corn does not, so in each county the irrigated yield should be the higher one. So ask:
Using the table corn, for each county with one irrigated and one
non-irrigated row, check whether the irrigated yield is higher. Print
how many counties pass and how many fail.
The AI’s code, and what it printed:


Code the AI wrote
corn |>
  group_by(FIPS) |>
  filter(n() == 2, n_distinct(Irrigated) == 2) |>
  summarise(irrigated_higher = Yield[Irrigated == 1] > Yield[Irrigated == 0]) |>
  count(irrigated_higher)


# A tibble: 1 × 2
  irrigated_higher     n
  <lgl>            <int>
1 TRUE                70


All 70 counties pass. A row count or a type check could never have tested this; only what you know about corn could.
When a check like this fails, the code is usually not the problem: the file is. Stop, and ask whoever produced the file before you analyse it.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Your turn: read the AI’s code
text:
Your turn: read the AI’s code
A student asked an AI to “load corn_yields.xls and compute the average yield”, and got this:

setwd("C:/Users/jsmith/Desktop/class")
library(readxl)
corn <- read_excel("corn_yields.xls")
mean(corn$Yield)


QuestionsAnswers


A. What does each of the four lines do?
B. Which line will fail on your computer, and why?
C. Which problem would give a wrong answer without an error?
D. Rewrite the request so the AI could not make these mistakes.


A. Changes the working directory; loads readxl; reads the workbook into corn; averages the Yield column.
B. Line 1. The folder C:/Users/jsmith/... exists only on jsmith’s computer.
C. Line 3 reads only the first sheet, so corn holds 2008 only, and nothing says so. The average leaves out 2009.
D. Name both sheets, say whether you want both years or one, ask for here::here() and no setwd(), and ask it to print the row count per sheet.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
text:
How writing code is written
Writing (exporting) is reading in reverse: a function takes a table from R and saves it as a file. Again, every writer follows the same pattern.

The patternEvery writer follows the patternA default that surprisesChoosing a format



writer_function(table_name, "path/to/file", option = value, ...)









Part
What it is
Required?




writer_function
The function that writes this format
Yes


table_name
The table to save, always the first input
Yes


"path/to/file"
Where to save it, always the second input
Yes


option = value
Extra instructions, such as how to write missing values
No; each has a default



Two differences from reading:

There is no table_name <- in front. The result is a file on disk, not a new table in R.
If a file already exists at that path, it is replaced without asking. Writing to the same path as your raw data destroys the raw data.






Format
Shortest call
Package




csv
write_csv(corn, "corn.csv")
readr (tidyverse)


csv
write.csv(corn, "corn.csv")
built into R


Excel
write_xlsx(corn, "corn.xlsx")
writexl


STATA
write_dta(corn, "corn.dta")
haven


R’s own
saveRDS(corn, "corn.rds")
built into R



The same variations as for reading appear here too: readr::write_csv(...), and the path built with here::here(...).


Defaults matter when writing too. The built-in write.csv() adds a column of row numbers by default. Read the file back, and that column returns as an extra column:

tmp <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn_base.csv")
write.csv(corn, tmp)
names(read.csv(tmp))

 [1] "X"           "Year"        "State"       "FIPS"        "County_name"
 [6] "State_name"  "Commodity"   "Data.item"   "Irrigated"   "Yield"      


The extra first column, X, holds 1, 2, 3, and so on. Adding row.names = FALSE prevents it; write_csv() never adds it. When the AI writes write.csv(), check for that option.
Notice also that Data item came back as Data.item. That one is a default of the reader: read.csv() replaces spaces in column names with dots, and read_csv() does not.


The decision that is yours is the format, and it depends on who reads the file next and what has to survive:








Format
Choose it when
What is lost




csv
anyone, in any software, must be able to read it
every type: dates, factors (columns of categories) and text IDs come back as guesses


rds
you, in R, will read it in the next step of the project
nothing, but only R can open it


dta
a collaborator uses STATA
some R-only types







A reasonable default


Keep raw data as you received it. Save intermediate results as rds, so types survive from one script to the next.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
section: Checking an export: the round trip
text:
Checking an export: the round trip
Why: a file can quietly keep less than you saved. The only way to know what it kept is to read it back.
What to ask: “Save the table, read it back, and compare it with the original.” Here Irrigated was first made a factor, then saved as csv and as rds:


Code the AI wrote
corn_f <- mutate(corn, Irrigated = factor(Irrigated, labels = c("no", "yes")))

csv_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.csv")
rds_file <- file.path(tempdir(), "corn.rds")
write_csv(corn_f, csv_file)
saveRDS(corn_f, rds_file)

c(
  from_csv = class(read_csv(csv_file, show_col_types = FALSE)$Irrigated),
  from_rds = class(readRDS(rds_file)$Irrigated)
)


   from_csv    from_rds 
"character"    "factor" 


The csv gave back text: the factor was lost. The rds gave back the factor.
The request is under Recommended requests, tab “Save and read back”.

title: 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R
text:
Requests you can copy
Copy one, then replace every <...> with what you found by looking at the file. The blanks are the part the AI cannot fill in for you. Every request for code ends with the closing instructions.

Closing instructionsLook at a fileRead a csvRead an Excel workbookSave and read backExplain code


The lines that end every request for code. Replace the two blanks; leave “expected X, got Y” as it is, because it tells the AI how to print each check:
Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.
A chat assistant cannot render: paste its chunks into your .qmd and render it yourself. An agent in your editor or terminal can do every step.


Without reading <path to the file> as a table, show me its first
<number> raw lines and the total number of lines.

Put the code in my Quarto document <path to your .qmd>, under the
heading "<heading>", as R code chunks. Above each chunk, write one
plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <path to the file> is a csv file. I looked at it:
- above the column names there is <what is there, or nothing>
- there are <number> data rows and <number> columns
- one row is <what one row is>
- missing values are written as <how they are written>
- ID columns that must stay text: <ID columns>

Read it into a table called <table name> using the tidyverse. Then check
the number of rows and columns, the type of every column, the number of
missing values in each column, the range of <column>, and the first row.

plain-English sentence saying what it does and why. Build every path
with here::here(); no setwd(), no absolute paths. Print each check on
its own line as "name of check: expected X, got Y". Render the document
to HTML.


In my R project, <path to the file> is an Excel workbook with the
sheets <sheet names>. I want <which sheets, and whether to stack them
into one table>, in a table called <table name>. Each sheet has
<number> rows, and <column> tells the sheets apart. ID columns that
must stay text: <ID columns>.

Then check the number of rows from each sheet and in total, the type of

values of <column that tells the sheets apart>.

to HTML.


Save the table <table name> as <path for the new file, ending in .rds or
.csv>. Then read the file back and tell me, in one plain-English line,
whether it matches the original exactly, and if not, which columns
differ and how.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 03-1: Getting Data In and Out of R. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: knowing what the files contain, asking for the right thing and the right checks, and judging whether the result is right.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 162 lines: one line of column names and 161 data rows.
B. 9 columns: Year, State, FIPS, County_name, State_name, Commodity, Data item, Irrigated, Yield. County_name, State_name, Commodity and Data item are text; the rest are numbers. Data item has a space in its name.
C. One county, one year, and one irrigation status (Irrigated is 0 or 1), so most counties appear twice.
D. Two sheets, corn_yields_08 and corn_yields_09.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 2: Read the csv






What you should find





161 rows and 9 columns, no missing values, and yields from 103 to 204 bushels per acre.
The checks, and why. The five from the lecture, each tied to a way this import could go wrong:

Rows and columns: a title line read as data, or the reader stopping early, changes the count from the 161 you counted.
Type of every column: Yield read as text would make every later calculation fail or mislead.
Missing values per column: a column that failed to read shows up as all missing.
Range of Yield: a code such as -999, or a number in the wrong units, shows up as an impossible value.
The first row: shifted columns show up when compared with the first data line of the file.

The blanks of the recommended request, filled in:
- above the column names there is nothing
- there are 161 data rows and 9 columns
- one row is one county, one year, and one irrigation status
- missing values are written as: none expected
- ID columns that must stay text: FIPS
- a believable range for Yield is 100 to 250
In the HTML, every “expected, got” line should match.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file
text:
Task 3: Both sheets of the Excel file






What you should find





161 + 161 = 322 rows. Year is 2008 in one sheet and 2009 in the other.
The check from knowing the data. Yields change from year to year, because the weather does, so each county’s yield should differ between the two years. Asking “is each county’s yield the same in both years?” gives TRUE: every county has exactly the same yield.
That cannot be real data. The code is fine; the file is wrong, and no change to the code fixes it. The right move is to stop and ask whoever produced the file, and not to analyse year-to-year changes until you have an answer.
This is the point of the task: the row count and the types all passed. Only a check you thought of, because you know something about corn, caught the problem.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 4: A messy file






What you should find





4a, the short request. Plain read_csv() treats the first description line as the column names, so you get 94 rows and only 3 columns with sentence fragments for names, plus a warning about parsing problems. Base R’s read.csv() stops with an error instead. Either way the problem is visible, which is the good case.
4b, the file. Two lines of description sit above the column names. Missing yields are written two ways, -999 and ., and the second description line says so. county_fips holds 5-digit county codes, and the 5 Colorado codes start with 08. There are 95 lines, so 92 data rows.
4c, a correct result. 92 rows, 5 columns, county_fips is text with the leading zeros kept, yield is a number, 5 yields are missing, and the rest run from 102 to 199. Average yield: 157.7.
The checks, and the problem each one catches in this file:

Rows: the description lines read as data.
Type of county_fips: the leading 0 of the Colorado codes lost.
Type of the yield column: text instead of a number, because of the . entries.
Number of missing yields: should be 5. Fewer means a missing-value code was kept as a value.
Range of yields: a minimum of -999 means the -999 code was not recognised.

The silent trap. If your request mentioned . but not -999, the yield column is a number, nothing errors, and the average comes out at 119.2. Checks 4 and 5 both catch it.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 5: Maria’s code






Answers





A. Read the file, skipping the two description lines and treating . as missing; rename the fifth column to yield; average the yields, ignoring missing ones.
B. The path. C:/Users/maria/Downloads exists only on Maria’s computer.
C. First, -999 is not treated as missing, so the average is 119.2 instead of 157.7. Second, read.csv() reads county_fips as a number, so 08125 becomes 8125. Nothing uses that column here, but the first time Maria joins this table to another one by county code, the Colorado counties will quietly fail to match.
D. “Print the smallest and largest yield”: a minimum of -999 is impossible. “Print the type of every column”: county_fips should be text, because it is an ID, not a quantity.
E. The AI usually spots the path and often the -999. It can only spot the -999 because the code itself is visible to it; it has not seen the file. Whether it notices the lost leading zero varies. Either way, compare its list with yours, and treat its answer like any other: something to check, not something to accept.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 6: Save and read back






What you should find





The rds file comes back identical. The csv file comes back with state_name as plain text rather than a factor, because a csv stores only text and the reader has to guess types again. This is why the lecture recommends rds for results you will read back into R.
If the AI compares with all.equal(), the csv comparison prints several lines starting with Attributes: before the one that matters, Component "state_name": 'current' is not a factor. The Attributes lines are about hidden bookkeeping that read_csv() attaches to every table it reads, not about your data. Ask the AI which lines are about the data itself if this is unclear.

title: Ex-3-1: Getting Data In and Out, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 7: Does it run anywhere?






What you should find





If it fails on your neighbour’s computer, the error names the line that depended on your machine, almost always a path. Ask the AI to fix that line, explaining what failed, and try again. A worksheet that renders on someone else’s computer unchanged is the final check that every path in it is relative to the project.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text: This is an in-class exercise. Before class, work through the lecture 04-1: Communicating with Figures. In class, you work through the worksheet with an AI assistant writing the code. Your job is everything the AI cannot do: deciding what each figure must say and to whom, choosing among the designs the AI offers, and judging the result in the rendered HTML.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 1: Look and predict






What you should find





A. 1,957 lines: one line of column names and 1,956 data rows, 6 columns. One row is one county in one year.
B. 3 states (Colorado, Kansas, Nebraska), 154 counties (some county names, such as Lincoln, occur in more than one state, so a county is identified by its state and its name), years 2000 to 2018.
C. corn_yield runs from 0 to 234.3 bushels per acre. The 2 zeros are odd: both are in Colorado (Bent 2003 and Elbert 2002), and the next lowest yield anywhere is 80. A zero could be a crop that failed completely, or a missing value written as 0. The file cannot tell you which. Note it, and keep it in mind for any figure of yields. drought_weeks runs from 0 to 22.
D. The table of counties per state and year shows two things:

Colorado has no rows at all for 2009.
The number of counties falls over time. Kansas has 56 counties in 2000 and 2 in 2008. Colorado has 5 or fewer counties in 7 of its years.

Any average per state and year is therefore an average over a different, sometimes very small, set of counties. Task 7 comes back to this.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 2: Write the message






What a good answer looks like





Average yields in 2000 to 2002 and in 2016 to 2018:



State
2000 to 2002

So yields rose in all three states, most in Nebraska. A good sentence states the direction, the scope and if possible a size: “Corn yields rose in all three states between 2000 and 2018, by about 26 to 47 bushels per acre.” A sentence such as “Yields changed over time” is not a message; nothing in a figure could show it to be wrong.
The reader matters for the wording and the labels: an extension audience knows bushels per acre; a general audience needs it spelled out once.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 3: Ask for designs and choose
text:
Task 3: Ask for designs and choose






What a good answer looks like





Designs you may get back include:

One line per state, yearly average. Makes the rise and the comparison between states easy to see. Hides how much counties vary within a year, and each point is an average over a changing set of counties (Task 7).
Small panels per state, every county-year as a point, with a trend line. Shows the rise and the spread, and how few Colorado points there are. Harder to compare the states’ levels at a glance.
Box plots per year. Shows the spread each year, but mixes the states, so it cannot show “in all three states”.

For the sentence in Task 2, one line per state, or panels per state with a trend line, serve the message; box plots per year do not, because the message is about each state. A good written reason names what the message needs (“each state separately, over time”) and what the chosen design makes easy to see.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 4: Meet the figure standard






What to check in the HTML





Go through the eight items one at a time, in the HTML, not in the code:

Axis titles in words with units: “Corn yield (bushels per acre)”. The years need no axis title. Nothing like corn_yield or state_name anywhere.
Tick labels and axis titles at least as large as the worksheet’s text.
Lines labelled at their ends, or a legend in an empty corner in the order of the lines at the right edge.
Numbers: years printed as 2000, not 2,000 or 2000.0.
No overlapping years along the bottom; every second or fifth year is fine.
Light or no gridlines.
Wider than tall, since this is a change over time.
Colourblind-safe colours, one per state. If you kept colours from earlier figures, the same state has the same colour.

Check every item even though your request listed them all. A request says what you asked for, not what you got.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure
text:
Task 5: Critique and improve a weak figure






What a good answer looks like





The numbers behind the message. County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought, compared with county-years with none:








State
Yield lower by (bushels per acre)
County-years with over 10 weeks




Colorado

The message is true for all three states.
The checklist, applied to the weak figure:

Message in a few seconds: no. 1,956 points pile up, and most of them sit in one column at zero weeks.
Colour carries information (the state), but the three states’ points are mixed together in one cloud, and where they overlap, Nebraska’s, drawn last, hide the others. The reader cannot compare the states.
In black and white: no, the states become indistinguishable.
Everything shown is needed, but the comparison the message needs, yields with and without long drought in each state, is not shown.
Figure standard: raw column names, small text, ggplot’s default red and green, a legend to the right.

A good improvement puts the comparison the message needs in front of the reader. Two that work: one small panel per state showing yields per drought range (box plots or averages); or one point per state for “no drought” and one for “over 10 weeks”, joined by a line, so the drop is the length of the line. The first shows the spread too; the second makes the size of the drop easiest to read. Either, with a reason, is a good answer.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
text:
Task 6: Is the message true?






What you should find





2012 was a drought year everywhere: on average 12.4 weeks of extreme drought per county in Colorado, 11.5 in Kansas and 9.1 in Nebraska. But the yields did not all fall:

Nebraska’s average yield was higher in 2012 than in 2011, and Kansas’s did not change, because 2011 was already a poor year in Kansas (8.4 bushels per acre below its counties’ own averages). The draft message is false for Nebraska, and no design can fix a false message. The data does not say why; it has no information on irrigation, for example.
Because the set of counties changes from year to year, a careful check compares each county with its own average over all years. That gives the same picture: in 2012, Colorado counties were 15.6 bushels per acre below their own average, Kansas counties 12.6 below, and Nebraska counties 2.6 above.
A true message, for example: “In the 2012 drought, yields were below normal in Colorado and Kansas but not in Nebraska.” It is about one year and a difference from normal, so a good design is different from Task 3’s: for example, a bar per state showing 2012’s yield minus normal, coloured on two hues either side of zero, or the Task 3 lines with 2012 marked. Colorado’s 2012 value rests on only 4 counties, which belongs in a note under the figure.

title: Ex-4-1: Communicating with Figures, with an AI Assistant
section: Task 7: Check the figure against its data
text:
Task 7: Check the figure against its data






What you should find





For one line per state, the expected table has 3 states × 19 years = 57 rows. It has 56: Colorado 2009 is missing, and a line drawn from this table joins 2008 straight to 2010 without showing it.
The counties behind each point range from 2 to 82. Colorado’s points rest on 5 or fewer counties in 7 of its years.
What to do about it is your decision, and several answers are good, as long as the figure or its note tells the reader:

break the line at the missing year, so the gap is visible;
show the number of counties, for example as the size of each point, or in a note under the figure;
compare each county with its own average, so a point does not depend on which counties report that year.

Doing nothing and saying nothing is the one answer that is not good.

title: Data Science with R for Environmental, Agricultural, and Social Scientists
text: Course materials for Data Science with R (AECN 896-05) at UNL, redesigned for working alongside AI. The lectures teach what each step of a data project is, what has to be true for it to succeed, what to ask an AI assistant to do, and how to check what comes back.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What you will and will not learn today
text:
What you will and will not learn today

The planDirections


An AI assistant can draw any figure in seconds. It knows every function and every option. What it cannot know is:

what the figure is supposed to tell the reader
who the reader is, and what they already know
which group or which year the message is about
whether the finished figure gets the message across

Those four are your job. So today is about:

The concept: a figure exists to convey one fact or idea, and every design choice is judged against it
Reading code: recognising which line of figure code does what, without memorising it
Asking AI: what to put in a figure request
Checking: how to judge whether a figure is correct and whether it conveys its message




Ask your AI assistant to install the tidyverse package if you have not already. It includes ggplot2, the package that draws every figure in this course.
The figures use county_yield.csv, which you can download from the page of exercise 4-1. One row is one county in one year: corn yield and weeks of drought for 154 counties in Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska, 2000 to 2018.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
One sentence and one reader

What you needWhy the AI cannot do this


Before you ask for any figure, write down two things:

The message: the one sentence the reader should take away. A finding, with a direction and if possible a size: “County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought yielded about 22 bushels per acre less than county-years with none.”
The reader: who will look at the figure, and what they already know. A farm audience knows what a bushel per acre is; a general audience may not.

How to tell it is done: someone who sees only the figure, without your text, can say your sentence back to you.


The same table supports many sentences. Asked for “a figure of this data”, the AI has to choose a message without knowing yours, and it usually picks the figure that suits the types of the columns, not the point you want to make.
Every design decision in this lecture (type of figure, colour, order, axis range, title) is judged against your sentence. Without the sentence, there is nothing to judge against.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
The message decides the figure
Both figures are drawn from the same 1,956 rows. Each serves a different sentence.

Message AMessage B


“County-years with more than 10 weeks of extreme drought yielded about 22 bushels per acre less than county-years with none.”











“Extreme drought came in a few bad years, above all 2012 and 2013.”

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
The shape every figure shares
You will not write figure code from memory. You need to look at any figure code the AI writes and say which column is shown by what, because that is where a figure goes wrong. Every ggplot2 figure has the same shape.

The patternOne real exampleEvery mark has this shapeInside or outside aes()Variations you will see



ggplot(table, aes(x = column, y = column, colour = column)) +
  geom_mark() +
  optional_layer() +
  optional_layer()









Part
What it is
Required?




ggplot(table, ...)

Yes


aes(...)
Which column is shown by which visual property: position on the x axis, position on the y axis, colour, size (aes stands for aesthetics, ggplot’s word for visual properties)
Yes


geom_mark()
The kind of mark drawn: geom_point(), geom_line(), geom_col() and so on
Yes, at least one


+
Adds the next layer. It ends a line; a line never starts with it
Between layers


optional_layer()
Axis and legend titles (labs()), colours and axis ranges (scale_...()), small panels (facet_...()), text size and gridlines (theme())
No; each has a default



How to tell you can read it: for any figure code, you can fill in a table with one row per column of the data that is used, saying what it sets in the figure.


state_year has one row per state and year, with the average corn yield of the counties in the data.

ggplot(state_year, aes(x = year, y = corn_yield, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_colours) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Average corn yield\n(bushels per acre)", colour = NULL)

The mark is lines. The two optional layers set the three colours and the axis and legend titles.


Marks differ in name, not in shape. The visual properties each one needs inside aes():



Mark
In the code

Any of them also accepts colour, fill (the colour inside a bar or box), size, shape (of points) and linetype inside aes().


The same word means two different things depending on where it is written:

Inside aes(): aes(colour = state_name) means “the colour depends on the column state_name”, and ggplot adds a legend.
Outside aes(): geom_line(colour = "grey40") means “every line is grey”. No column is involved, and there is no legend.

Writing a fixed colour inside aes() is a common slip. ggplot treats "blue" as a column whose value is the word “blue”, gives it the first default colour, and adds a legend for it:

ggplot(band_means, aes(band, corn_yield)) +
  geom_point(aes(colour = "blue"), size = 4)








No error, and the points are not blue.


AI-written code often writes the same pattern differently. These change how the code looks, not what it draws:

aes(year, corn_yield): without x = and y =. The first two inputs are x and y.
ggplot(data = cy, mapping = aes(...)): the input names spelled out.
cy |> ggplot(aes(...)): the table passed in with |> instead of written first.
geom_point(aes(colour = state_name)): the aes() inside one mark instead of in ggplot(). It then applies to that mark only.
p <- ggplot(...) + geom_line() on one line, then p + labs(...) later: the figure is stored under a name and added to.

A + at the start of a line stops R with the error “Cannot use + with a single argument”. The fix is to move it to the end of the line above.

text:
Five kinds of message

The tableDistributionPart of a whole


The kind of sentence you wrote tells you the kind of figure to start from. The last column is the part of the code that names the figure type, so you can recognise it in what the AI writes.









Kind of message
A sentence from this data
A figure that suits it
In the code

“Half of all county-years yielded between 164 and 195 bushels per acre.”
histogram

“Yields fall as drought lasts longer.”
points, or averages per range
geom_point()

“Nebraska counties typically yield more than Kansas or Colorado counties.”

geom_boxplot(), geom_col()


A change over time
“Extreme drought came in 2012 and 2013.”

The next two slides take a comparison and a relationship and show how much the choice matters.


“Half of all county-years yielded between 164 and 195 bushels per acre.”









The shaded band is the middle half. The handful of yields near zero are real rows; the exercise asks what they are.


“Nebraska makes up 65% of the county-years.”

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
One message, three figures
Message: “Nebraska counties typically yield more corn than Kansas or Colorado counties.”

A. Overlapping histogramsB. Box plotsC. Bars of the averageWhich one?











Nebraska has the most rows, so its histogram covers the other two. The reader sees “Nebraska is big”, which is a fact about the data, not about yields.











The thick line in each box is the median (half the counties yield more, half less), and the box holds the middle half. Nebraska’s median is 184, against 174 for Kansas and 172 for Colorado, and the boxes show how much the states overlap.











The bars are correct, but they make the states look alike: Nebraska’s average (182) is only 8% above Colorado’s (168), so the difference is a sliver at the end of a long bar.


B serves this message. “Typically” is a statement about the middle of each state’s yields, and box plots put the middle and the spread side by side.

A hides the comparison under the difference in the number of rows.
C shows the averages but no spread, so the reader cannot tell whether the gap is large compared with the variation inside each state.

For another message, say “Colorado has the most variable yields”, B still works, while C would not show it at all.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
Too many points
Message: “Yields fall when drought lasts longer.”

A. Every county-yearB. Box plots per drought range











73% of the county-years had no extreme drought, so most points sit on top of each other in one column at zero. The fall is there, but the eye cannot find it.











Grouping the drought weeks into ranges shows the drop at once. It also shows that the fall is not steady: the “2 to 5” group does better than the “0 to 2” group. Your sentence should not claim more than the figure shows; “yields are lowest after more than 10 weeks of drought” is what this figure supports.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
When colour should carry information

The ruleDecorationInformation


Use colour only for a variable the reader needs and that the position of the marks does not already show. How to tell: remove the colour in your head. If the reader loses nothing, the colour is decoration, and decoration makes the reader look for a meaning that is not there.











Each state already has its own place on the horizontal axis. The colours and the legend repeat the axis labels.











Three lines share one pair of axes. Colour is the only thing that says which line is which state.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
Three kinds of colour scale

CategoriesAmountsAbove or below a midpoint


Groups with no order (states, crops) get clearly different hues, as in the line figure on the previous slide. Use as few as the message needs.


Amounts (weeks of drought, yield) get one hue, from light for small to dark for large, so “darker means more” reads without a legend.











A value above or below a meaningful middle (a change, a difference from normal) gets two hues that grow darker away from a neutral middle. Here, each county’s yield minus its own 2000 to 2018 average, averaged over the counties of each state:









Orange is below normal, purple above, and pale means close to normal. The neutral middle must sit at the value that means “no difference”, here zero.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Highlight the group the message is about
text:
Highlight the group the message is about

HighlightSame colour, same thing


Message: “Colorado’s 2002 drought lasted about twice as long as Kansas’s or Nebraska’s.”









In 2002: Colorado 15.3 weeks, Kansas 6.5, Nebraska 7.3. The other states stay in the figure, in grey, because the message is a comparison with them.


Every figure on this deck draws Colorado in orange, Kansas in blue and Nebraska in green, including the highlight, where Colorado keeps its orange. A reader who learns the colours on one figure can read the next one without the legend.
Left to its defaults, ggplot hands out colours to whichever groups are in each figure, in alphabetical order. A figure without Colorado gives Kansas the colour Colorado had in the figure before. Name the colours in your request: “Colorado #E69F00, Kansas #0072B2, Nebraska #009E73 in every figure”.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Colours every reader can tell apart
text:
Colours every reader can tell apart

ggplot’s defaultAs a red-green colour-blind reader sees itOkabe-Ito, as the same reader sees itHow many colours


A deliberately bad example. ggplot’s default colours for three groups put a red and a green of about the same lightness next to each other:











The same figure, with its colours converted to what a reader with red-green colour blindness sees (simulated with the colorspace package):









Colorado and Kansas now look nearly the same.


The Okabe-Ito palette is a set of eight colours chosen to stay distinct for colour-blind readers. The colours used for the states on this deck come from it:











A reader has to match each colour to the legend, and that gets unreliable well before a palette runs out. With more groups than you can give clearly different colours:

colour only the groups the message is about and grey the rest, or
draw one small panel per group (next section), or
combine the small groups into “Other”.

Check: would the message survive printing in black and white? If colour is the only thing separating two lines, label them directly too.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
Order categories by value
The 12 counties with data in every year, all in Nebraska. Message: “Buffalo had the highest average yield.”

Alphabetical, names along the bottomBy value, names down the side











The names crowd together until they almost touch, and finding the highest county means comparing every point with every other.











Ordered by value, the ranking is the figure. With the names on the vertical axis they read horizontally and never overlap. Rotating the names by 45 or 90 degrees would also stop the overlap, but makes them harder to read.
Keep the natural order when the categories have one: years, months, drought ranges from none to most.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
One panel or several
Message: “Nebraska’s yields sit higher than the other two states’.”

Several small panelsWhen to use which











The overlapping histograms from “One message, three figures”, split into one panel per state. Stacked one above the other on the same horizontal axis, the shift of Nebraska’s yields to the right is visible.



One panel when the reader must compare values at the same point, for example three lines in the same year. Up to about three or four groups.
Several small panels when the groups overlap so much that one panel becomes a tangle, or there are too many groups to colour.
Panels must share the axis the comparison is made on. Here the horizontal axis (yield) is shared; the vertical axis (counts) differs on purpose, because Nebraska has far more rows and the message is about where the yields sit, not how many rows each state has. Say so when you ask, or the AI decides for you.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
Axis ranges

Bars that do not start at zeroBars from zeroPoints and lines











A deliberately bad example. A bar’s length is read as its value. With the axis starting at 165, Nebraska’s bar is 5 times as tall as Colorado’s, although its average is only 8% higher.











Honest, and it shows the differences are small. If the message is about those small differences, bars are the wrong choice; use points, which need no zero.


For points and lines the reader reads position, not length, so the axis should cover the range where the variation that matters lies. The dot plot of county averages on the “Order categories by value” slide runs from about 183 to 197. Forced to start at zero, all 12 points would crowd into the right 7% of the panel’s width and the ranking would be hard to see.
The opposite mistake: an axis so narrow that a change too small to matter fills the whole figure. The range should match what the message calls large.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Titles, labels, and what to leave out
text:
Titles, labels, and what to leave out

A title that states the findingLabels on the linesRemove what the message does not need











A title such as “corn_yield by drought band” names the variables, which the axes already do. A title that states the finding tells the reader what to look for. In a report where the figure has a caption, the caption can carry the finding instead.


A legend makes the reader look away from the data, find the colour, read the name, and look back, once for every line. A label at the end of each line removes that trip. The “Highlight” figure in the colour section labels its lines directly; the before-and-after slide below does the same for three lines.
When there is only one group, there is nothing for a legend to explain. Remove it.


Look at each element and ask whether the message would suffer without it:

a legend that repeats the axis labels
colour that repeats position
heavy gridlines, a dark background, a box around the panel
numbers printed on every bar when the message is the ranking
a third dimension

What remains should be the data, the axes, and the words needed to read them.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
The figure standard
Every figure you hand in must meet this standard, whatever its message. Each item has a yes or no answer.

Plain-word labels. Axis titles and legend titles in plain words with units: “Corn yield (bushels per acre)”, never corn_yield. Category labels in words: “Irrigated”, not 1.
Readable text. Tick labels, axis titles and legend text no smaller than the document’s body text, at the size the figure appears in the HTML.
The legend where it costs least. In an empty corner of the plot, or above or below a wide figure, or removed when lines or points are labelled directly or there is only one group. Its order matches the order of the lines or bars.
Numbers formatted for reading. Thousands separators, no more decimals than the message needs, percentages shown as percentages.
No overlapping tick labels. For long category names, put the categories on the vertical axis.
The data is the darkest thing. Light or no gridlines, no heavy borders.
A shape that suits the content. Wide for a change over time, close to square for a relationship between two variables.
Colours every reader can tell apart. A palette readable by colour-blind readers, and no more colours than the message needs.

The copyable version, to add to every figure request, is in Recommended requests at the end of this deck.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What must be true of the data
text:
What must be true of the data

The conditionsA year stored as a numberA year that is not thereThe check



One row per thing drawn. One row per point, per bar, or per point on a line. If the table has one row per county and the line is meant to show one value per state and year, the averaging must happen first.
The right type per column. A category the colour should separate (a year, an ID, a 0/1 code) must be stored as a category. Stored as a number, it gets a scale for amounts.
Nothing missing that the figure hides. A line joins whatever rows it is given, whether or not a year is missing between them.

None of these failures gives an error. The figure is drawn, and it is wrong.











The request was “colour the points by year” for three years. year is stored as a number, so ggplot drew a scale for an amount: a legend with shades for years that are not in the figure, and three shades of one blue that are hard to tell apart.











The data has no Colorado row for 2009. The orange line runs straight from 2008 to 2010 and nothing on the figure says a year is missing.


Ask the AI to print, next to the figure in the HTML, the table the figure is drawn from, with the number of original rows behind each value. Here, the rows around 2009:


Code the AI wrote
state_year_raw |>
  filter(year %in% 2008:2010) |>
  arrange(year, state_name) |>
  mutate(across(c(corn_yield, drought_weeks), \(x) round(x, 1)))

Two problems show at once. Colorado has no 2009 row. And Kansas’s 2008 average comes from 2 counties, against 26 in 2010: a point on that line can rest on very few counties. Neither is visible in the figure.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
The checklist
Apply it to any figure, yours or the AI’s, by looking at it in the rendered HTML, at the size a reader will see it. Each question has a yes or no answer.

Can someone who has not seen the data state the message within a few seconds?
Does every colour carry information? (No colour that only decorates.)
Would the message survive printing in black and white?
Is everything in the figure needed for the message?
Does it meet every item of the figure standard?
Does the table printed next to the figure have one row per thing drawn, with nothing missing that the figure hides?

A “no” to any question is something to fix or a reason to choose a different design.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
text:
Your turn: judge a figure
The message is meant to be: “Extreme drought came in a few bad years, above all 2012 and 2013.”


QuestionsAnswers


A. Apply questions 1 to 5 of the checklist. Which answers are “no”?
B. What does the colour show that the position of the bars does not?
C. List the changes you would ask for, in the order that matters most for the message.


A. Question 1 is close to “yes”: the tall bars are visible. Question 2 is “no”, question 4 is “no” (the colour and its legend), and question 5 is “no”: raw column names as axis titles, text far smaller than the slide’s, a grey background.
B. Nothing. The colour repeats the year, which the horizontal axis already shows, and its legend narrows the plot.
C. Remove the colour and the legend; put the finding in the title; plain-word axis title with units (“Weeks of extreme drought, May to September”); larger text; no grey background. Bars are a reasonable choice here, since the values are counts of weeks and start at zero; a line would also do.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: Working with AI on your own research
text:
Working with AI on your own research
Figures follow the same way of working as everything else (lecture 03-1, “Working with AI on your own research”): you ask, the AI writes into a Quarto document, you render, and you judge the HTML.
For figures, judging the HTML matters even more:

A figure’s text size, shape and legend only exist at the size it is shown. The chat window shows it at a different size, or not at all.
The figure sits next to the sentence that says what it shows, so you can check that the two agree.
The table the figure is drawn from can be printed right next to it.

Every figure request ends with the figure standard and then the closing instructions. Both are under Recommended requests.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: What to put in a figure request
text:
What to put in a figure request
The AI already knows how to draw any figure. Your request supplies what it cannot know:

The data: the file, what one row is, and which columns the figure uses, with their units
The message: the one sentence the reader should take away
The reader: who will see it, and what they already know
What matters: which group or which years the message is about, and colours that must stay fixed across figures
Alternatives, not one answer: two or three designs to choose from (next slide)
The figure standard, then the closing instructions





Using an agent in your editor or terminal?


An agent such as Claude Code can open the data and look for itself. It still cannot know your message or your reader. Write those down before it runs.

title: 04-1: Communicating with Figures
section: A weak request and a strong one
text:
A weak request and a strong one

WeakStrongWhat came back


Make a plot of my corn data.
The AI has to guess which columns, which message, which reader and which type of figure. Whatever it draws is a figure of the data, not of a message, and you have no sentence to judge it against.


In my R project, data/county_yield.csv has one row per county and year,
2000 to 2018, for Colorado, Kansas and Nebraska. drought_weeks is the
number of weeks from May to September the county spent in extreme
drought.

The message: extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in
2012 and 2013. The reader: an extension audience who knows the states
but has not seen this data.

Average drought_weeks by state and year, and draw one line per state
over time. Colorado #E69F00, Kansas #0072B2, Nebraska #009E73. Print
the table the figure is drawn from, with the number of counties behind
each value.
followed by the figure standard and the closing instructions.


A version of what an AI returns, the code behind the “After” figure. You should be able to say which part does what:

last_points <- filter(state_year, year == max(year))

ggplot(state_year, aes(year, drought_weeks, colour = state_name)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  ggrepel::geom_text_repel(
    data = last_points, aes(label = state_name),
    direction = "y", hjust = 0, nudge_x = 0.4, size = 5.5, seed = 1
  ) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = state_colours, guide = "none") +
  scale_x_continuous(
    breaks = seq(2000, 2018, 2),
    expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0.12))
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Extreme drought hit all three states in 2002, and again in 2012 and 2013",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Weeks of extreme drought,\nMay to September"
  )


ggplot(...) with aes(...): which column goes on which axis, and which column sets the colour
geom_line(): draw lines; geom_text_repel(): the labels at the line ends
scale_colour_manual(): the fixed colours, and guide = "none" removes the legend
labs(): the title and the axis titles

Requests you can copy
